questions.question: If n is the product of two distinct large primes p, q, how hard is factoring believed to be classically?
options: Sub-exponential: best known is GNFS, time exp(O((log n)^(1/3) (log log n)^(2/3)))
Polynomial: AKS factors n in time O(log^12 n) similar to its primality test
Exponential: no algorithm runs in time better than O(2^(log n)) on average
Linear: trial division up to √n finishes in O(n^(1/2)) wall-clock seconds
questions.explanation: GNFS (General Number Field Sieve) is sub-exponential, the asymptotic record. AKS factors nothing (it's a primality test). Trial division is √n — too slow for cryptographic sizes.

questions.question: What is the birthday paradox bound for collisions in a set of size N?
options: Expected collision after sampling ~√N elements at random with replacement
Expected collision after sampling ~log N elements at random with replacement
Expected collision only after sampling all N elements at least once each
Expected collision after sampling N/2 elements assuming uniform distribution
questions.explanation: Birthday: ~√N samples suffice for a collision with constant probability. Pollard-rho uses this to find x ≡ y (mod p) inside Z/nZ.

questions.question: How does Pollard's rho algorithm find a factor of n?
options: Iterate x ← f(x) mod n; gcd(|x_i − x_j|, n) > 1 reveals a factor when x_i ≡ x_j (mod p)
Trial-divide n by every prime up to n^(1/3), with random skipping for speed
Compute (a^k − 1) mod n for k = lcm(1..B); gcd of result with n gives a factor
Run Miller-Rabin until n is declared composite, then output the smallest witness
questions.explanation: Pollard-rho: iterate x ← x²+c (mod n). By birthday, expect cycle in Z/pZ after ~√p ≈ n^(1/4) steps. gcd of difference with n yields p.

questions.question: What is the expected time complexity of Pollard's rho on n = p·q with p < q?
options: O(p^(1/2)·polylog n) — Birthday bound on the smaller prime p
O(n^(1/2)·polylog n) — Same as trial division up to √n exactly
O(p·polylog n) — Linear in the smaller prime factor p of n
O(log^2 n) — Polynomial because Pollard-rho runs deterministically
questions.explanation: Pollard-rho finds smallest prime factor p in expected O(√p) iterations ≈ n^(1/4) for balanced semiprimes.

questions.question: Pollard's `p − 1` algorithm factors `n = p·q` efficiently when:
options: `p − 1` is B-smooth for some small bound B; then a^(B!) ≡ 1 (mod p) and gcd(a^(B!) − 1, n) = p
`p` and `q` are close to each other; Fermat factorization finds them via √n
`p + 1` factors into small primes; then ECM converges in O(log² n) steps
`p` is a safe prime of the form `2p′ + 1`; safe primes are special-attack-prone
questions.explanation: Pollard p−1: if p−1 = ∏ small primes ≤ B, then for any a coprime to p, a^M ≡ 1 (mod p) where M = lcm(1..B). gcd(a^M − 1, n) = p. Defense: choose p with large prime factor of p−1 ('safe' or 'strong' primes).

questions.question: Brent's improvement to Pollard-rho does what?
options: Replaces tortoise-and-hare cycle detection with a smarter scheme using ~24% fewer iterations
Adds quadratic sieving as a fallback when the rho loop exceeds expected √p time
Uses elliptic curves to speed up gcd computation inside the main rho iteration
Caches all previous x values to detect non-cycle collisions across attempts
questions.explanation: Brent's cycle detection replaces Floyd's tortoise-and-hare with a power-of-two stride. ~24% faster, same asymptotic.

questions.question: Find the factors of n = 8051 using Pollard-rho with f(x) = x² + 1, x₀ = 2.
options: 89 and 91, since 8051 = 89·91 (verify: 89·91 = 8099 — incorrect)
71 and 113, since 8051 = 71·113 (verify: 71·113 = 8023 — incorrect)
59 and 137, since 8051 = 59·137 (verify: 59·137 = 8083 — incorrect)
questions.explanation: 8051 = 83 · 97. Pollard-rho with x²+1 typically finds 83 within a dozen iterations.

questions.question: Why must RSA primes p be 'safe' (with p − 1 having a large prime factor)?
options: Otherwise Pollard p−1 factors n if any chosen prime has B-smooth p − 1 structure
Otherwise Miller-Rabin liars exist for n with high probability across most bases
Otherwise AKS misclassifies n as prime during the key generation procedure
Otherwise φ(n) becomes a prime power, invalidating CRT decryption optimization
questions.explanation: Safe primes p = 2p′+1 ensure p−1 = 2p′ is not smooth. Defends against Pollard p−1 and Williams p+1. NIST and PKCS recommendations require strong primes for older RSA keygen.
